hooks.note: Swift CMAttitude?; the CoreMotion shim derives it from the rotation vector sensor.
Swift private let motionManager = CMMotionManager(), shared like on iOS by the tap to focus device motion updates and the GForceManager accelerometer updates.

hooks.new: motionManager.stopDeviceMotionUpdates(); manualFocusMotionAttitude = null; motionManager.deviceMotionUpdateInterval = 0.2; motionManager.startDeviceMotionUpdates(to = com.moblin.android.platform.coremotion.OperationQueue.main) { data, _ -> if (data == null) { return@startDeviceMotionUpdates }; val attitude = data.attitude; if (manualFocusMotionAttitude == null) { manualFocusMotionAttitude = attitude }; if (diffAngles(attitude.pitch, manualFocusMotionAttitude!!.pitch) > 10) { setAutoFocus() } else if (diffAngles(attitude.roll, manualFocusMotionAttitude!!.roll) > 10) { setAutoFocus() } else if (diffAngles(attitude.yaw, manualFocusMotionAttitude!!.yaw) > 10) { setAutoFocus() } }
hooks.note: Swift startMotionDetection on one line: back to continuous focus and exposure once the phone turns more than 10 degrees from where tap to focus was done.

iOS suspends the app in the background when nothing keeps it running, so its tap to focus motion updates stop with it; Android keeps the sensors on until the phone moves. Returning to the foreground attaches the camera and setAutoFocus() drops the tapped point either way.
Swift gForceManager = GForceManager(motionManager: motionManager); the accelerometer updates come from Model's CMMotionManager in g.
